specStatements.text: (HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current with the same frequency as the radio wave itself, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.
Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue. The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose. Radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.
Students will not be required to recall the unit of radiation dose.
Students should be able to draw conclusions from given data about the risks and consequences of exposure to radiation.
Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will not be required to recall the unit of radiation dose.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks the student to produce the name or symbol of the unit of radiation dose from memory. Wherever a dose appears — in a concept, a misconception or a question stem — the unit (sievert, Sv, or millisievert, mSv) is given to the student as part of the information supplied. The unit is used, converted and interpreted, which the specification does require through '1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)' and through drawing conclusions from given data, but it is never itself the answer to a recall question.

concepts.definition: A repeated back-and-forth change of the current in a circuit, so that the charges move first one way and then the other, over and over. (HT only) Oscillations of this kind in an electrical circuit can produce radio waves.
(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. The oscillating circuit is the source: the faster the oscillation, the higher the frequency of the radio wave produced.

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit. Production and absorption are therefore two directions of the same link between radio waves and oscillating circuits.

concepts.term: Frequency of the induced alternating current
concepts.definition: (HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 kHz radio wave absorbed by a circuit induces an alternating current of 200 kHz.

concepts.term: Atoms and nuclei as sources of electromagnetic waves
concepts.definition: Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same atom can therefore be involved in emitting or absorbing radiation from very different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. This origin, rather than any figure for frequency or wavelength, is what the specification uses to identify where gamma rays come from.

Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to radiation. It is not a count of the radiation itself: it combines how much radiation the body received with how damaging that type of radiation is.
The sievert is the unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose quoted in sieverts tells you about the risk of harm from an exposure, so a larger number of sieverts means a greater risk of harm.

A smaller unit of radiation dose, used for the everyday doses people actually receive. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so to convert a dose in mSv to Sv you divide by 1000, and to convert Sv to mSv you multiply by 1000.
X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation. Being ionising is what makes them hazardous to human body tissue: they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
Ultraviolet waves can have hazardous effects on human body tissue: they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
A change to a gene caused by ionising radiation. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

Using data you are given about radiation doses to compare exposures and comment on the risks and consequences. Doing this properly means converting all the doses to the same unit before comparing them, and stating conclusions as differences in risk rather than as certain outcomes.

misconceptions.question: Where do gamma rays come from?
misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma rays are given out by the electrons of an atom, in the same way that light is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet electrons moving and giving out radiation before they meet gamma rays, so they apply the picture they already have to every high-energy wave. Diagrams of atoms also draw attention to the electrons rather than the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: The specification distinguishes the two: changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can both produce electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, but gamma rays specifically originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

misconceptions.question: Do X-rays come from the nucleus, like gamma rays?
misconceptions.correct: Only gamma rays are stated to originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
misconceptions.misconception: If radiation is ionising it must have come out of the nucleus, so X-rays come from the nucleus too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: X-rays and gamma rays are named together as ionising radiation with similar hazards, so students assume they must also share an origin. 'Nuclear' and 'dangerous' become the same idea in their minds.
misconceptions.correction: Sharing a hazard is not sharing an origin. The specification names X-rays and gamma rays together as ionising radiation, but only gamma rays are said to originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

misconceptions.question: How are radio waves produced?
misconceptions.correct: (HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves come out of atoms, like the other electromagnetic waves do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once students learn that changes in atoms and nuclei generate electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, they generalise it to the whole spectrum and forget that the specification gives radio waves an electrical source.
misconceptions.correction: For radio waves the specification gives a circuit source: they can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. Only gamma rays are attributed to changes in the nucleus of an atom.

misconceptions.question: What is created in a circuit when a radio wave is absorbed?
misconceptions.correct: (HT only) An alternating current, with the same frequency as the radio wave itself.
misconceptions.misconception: The wave pushes charge one way, so it must produce a direct current in the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of absorption as the wave delivering a single push of energy, and their default picture of current from any supply is the steady, one-direction current of a cell.
misconceptions.correction: The wave oscillates, so the current it creates oscillates with it. When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current — the wave induces oscillations in the circuit.

misconceptions.question: What is the frequency of the current a radio wave induces?
misconceptions.correct: (HT only) The same frequency as the radio wave itself.
misconceptions.misconception: The circuit decides the frequency of the current, or the frequency gets halved or doubled on the way in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have seen a full wave cycle drawn as 'two pushes' count the pushes rather than the cycles, and others assume the receiving circuit imposes its own rate on whatever arrives.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 95 MHz wave induces a 95 MHz alternating current.

misconceptions.question: What does a radiation dose in sieverts tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: The dose just counts how much radiation there was — how many gamma rays hit you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Dose' sounds like a quantity of a substance, as with a dose of medicine, so students read it as an amount rather than as a measure of risk.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm from an exposure. It reflects both the size of the exposure and the type of radiation, because the effects depend on both.

misconceptions.question: How do you convert 2500 mSv into sieverts?
misconceptions.correct: Divide by 1000, because 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). 2500 mSv = 2.5 Sv.
misconceptions.misconception: The sievert is the bigger unit, so you multiply by 1000 to change millisieverts into sieverts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the two units differ by a factor of 1000 but not which way round, and 'bigger unit, so multiply' feels right without checking that it makes the answer absurdly large.
misconceptions.correction: Check the size of the answer. Since 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, a dose in mSv always gives a smaller number in Sv, so you divide by 1000.

misconceptions.question: Is ultraviolet ionising radiation?
misconceptions.correct: The specification names X-rays and gamma rays as ionising radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet must be ionising too, because it causes cancer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link the word 'cancer' to the word 'ionising' and treat them as the same statement, so any radiation described as causing cancer gets labelled ionising.
misconceptions.correction: Ultraviolet waves are hazardous — they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer — but it is X-rays and gamma rays that the specification identifies as ionising radiation causing the mutation of genes and cancer.

misconceptions.question: What do the hazardous effects of radiation depend on?
misconceptions.correct: The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the type of radiation that matters — gamma is dangerous and that is that, however much of it there is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The types are taught as a ranked list of hazards, which invites students to treat 'gamma' as a fixed level of danger and to drop the amount of exposure from the argument entirely.
misconceptions.correction: Both matter. The specification says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose, which is why dose is measured and recorded at all.

misconceptions.question: Why are X-rays and gamma rays hazardous to body tissue?
misconceptions.correct: They are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
misconceptions.misconception: They are hazardous because they heat the tissue up and burn it, like any strong wave would.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Heating is the effect students have already met for infrared and microwaves, so it becomes their general explanation for how any electromagnetic wave harms the body.
misconceptions.correction: The hazard named for X-rays and gamma rays is ionisation: they are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

misconceptions.question: Which is the larger dose, 800 mSv or 1.2 Sv?
misconceptions.correct: 1.2 Sv, because 1.2 Sv = 1200 mSv, which is larger than 800 mSv.
misconceptions.misconception: 800 is much bigger than 1.2, so 800 mSv must be the larger dose.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under time pressure students compare the numbers in front of them and treat the unit as a label rather than as part of the value, especially when one number is small and looks unimportant.
misconceptions.correction: Convert to a common unit before comparing. Using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, 1.2 Sv is 1200 mSv, so it is the larger dose and carries the greater risk of harm.

misconceptions.question: Does a large radiation dose mean the person will get cancer?
misconceptions.correct: A larger dose means a greater risk of harm, not a certain outcome.
misconceptions.misconception: If someone receives a big dose then they are definitely going to get cancer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Media reporting and the phrase 'radiation causes cancer' present the link as certain, and students have little experience of writing conclusions in terms of risk.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure. Conclusions drawn from dose data should be written as increased or decreased risk, never as a guaranteed consequence.

misconceptions.question: Is background radiation harmful?
misconceptions.correct: A background dose is a real exposure and carries a risk of harm, and is often the yardstick other doses are compared with.
misconceptions.misconception: Background radiation is natural, so it is harmless and can be left out when you compare doses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate 'natural' with 'safe', and background radiation is described as something everyone receives all the time, which makes it sound like nothing is happening.
misconceptions.correction: Dose measures risk of harm whatever the source. When drawing conclusions from data, background dose is included and is frequently the useful comparison — for example, expressing a scan as so many years' worth of background.

misconceptions.question: Do ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays affect the body in the same way?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultraviolet ages skin prematurely and increases skin cancer risk; X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
misconceptions.misconception: They are all hazardous, so they all do the same thing to the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three are listed together in one sentence about hazardous effects on human body tissue, so students store one hazard for the group instead of the specific effects the specification gives.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the effects separate. The specification states that the effects depend on the type of radiation, and gives the skin effects for ultraviolet and the ionising, gene-mutation effects for X-rays and gamma rays.

misconceptions.question: Is 2500 mSv the same as 2500 Sv?
misconceptions.correct: No. 2500 mSv = 2.5 Sv, because 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv).
misconceptions.misconception: Changing the unit does not change the number — you just swap mSv for Sv.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Prefixes are treated as decoration attached to the unit rather than as a factor, so students rewrite the unit and leave the value untouched.
misconceptions.correction: The prefix is a factor of 1000. Every conversion between mSv and Sv changes the number by 1000, so 2500 mSv becomes 2.5 Sv.

mcqs.stem: How can radio waves be produced?

options.text: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits.

options.text: By changes in the nucleus of an atom
options.rationale: A student who has generalised the nuclear origin of gamma rays to the whole spectrum picks the nucleus for radio waves as well.

options.text: By changes in the electrons of an atom
options.rationale: Chosen by students whose only model of wave emission is an electron changing in an atom, which they then apply to every part of the spectrum.

options.text: By heating a metal until it glows brightly
options.rationale: Heating is the source students associate with radiation from hot objects, so it is offered as a familiar but wrong mechanism for radio waves.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes what happens when a radio wave is absorbed by an electrical circuit?

options.text: It heats the circuit but produces no current at all
options.rationale: Picked by students who think absorption always means the energy simply ends up as heat, and who do not expect an electrical effect.

options.text: It creates a direct current in one fixed direction
options.rationale: The student's default picture of any current is the steady one-way current from a cell, so absorption is imagined as a single push.

options.text: It induces oscillations, creating an alternating current
options.rationale: When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current, so radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.

options.text: It creates a current whose frequency the circuit sets
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the receiving circuit imposes its own rate rather than following the frequency of the wave.

mcqs.stem: A transmitter circuit oscillates at 200 kHz and emits a radio wave. A distant circuit absorbs that wave. What alternating current is induced in the distant circuit?

options.text: 400 kHz, twice that of the radio wave
options.rationale: Students who count the two halves of each cycle as separate pushes double the frequency of the wave.

options.text: 200 kHz, the same as the radio wave
options.rationale: The alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself, so the 200 kHz wave induces a 200 kHz current.

options.text: 0 Hz, since a direct current is induced
options.rationale: Selected by students who believe an absorbed wave delivers a one-way push and therefore a steady, non-oscillating current.

options.text: 100 kHz, half that of the radio wave
options.rationale: A student who thinks energy is lost in transmission assumes the frequency drops as well, halving it as the obvious guess.

options.text: In changes in the nucleus of an atom
options.rationale: The specification states that gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.

options.text: In the vibration of the whole atom
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have a general picture of atoms vibrating and giving out radiation, without distinguishing which part of the atom changes.

options.text: In oscillations in an electrical circuit
options.rationale: Swaps the two sources given in this section, applying the radio-wave mechanism to gamma rays.

options.text: In changes in the electrons of an atom
options.rationale: The most common error: electrons are the part of the atom students picture changing, so gamma rays get attributed to them.

mcqs.stem: A student writes: 'X-rays must come from the nucleus, because they are ionising like gamma rays.' What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; all ionising radiation is nuclear
options.rationale: Students who treat 'ionising' and 'nuclear' as the same idea accept the argument as it stands.

options.text: Only gamma rays are stated to come from the nucleus
options.rationale: X-rays and gamma rays are named together as ionising radiation, but only gamma rays are attributed to changes in the nucleus of an atom.

options.text: Gamma rays come from the electrons, not the nucleus
options.rationale: Rejects the student's statement but for the wrong reason, using the common electron-origin error for gamma rays.

options.text: Gamma rays are not ionising, so the comparison fails
options.rationale: Chosen by students who misremember which radiations the specification names as ionising and so attack the wrong part of the claim.

mcqs.stem: What does a radiation dose, given in sieverts, measure?

options.text: The risk of harm from an exposure to radiation
options.rationale: Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation.

options.text: The frequency of the radiation absorbed
options.rationale: Frequency is the quantity students most often attach to radiation, so it is offered as the property being measured.

options.text: The number of gamma rays that reach the body
options.rationale: 'Dose' is read as an amount, like a dose of medicine, so the student expects it to be a count of radiation.

options.text: The type of radiation the body is exposed to
options.rationale: Students who think only the type of radiation matters assume the quantity recorded must be the type.

mcqs.stem: Two people are exposed to the same type of radiation, but one receives four times the dose of the other. What conclusion can be drawn?

options.text: The risk depends only on how long each exposure was
options.rationale: Time is confused with dose; the student replaces the quantity given with one that is not stated in the question.

options.text: The greater dose carries the greater risk of harm
options.rationale: The effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose, and dose measures the risk of harm, so the larger dose means the larger risk.

options.text: The risk is the same, as the type of radiation is the same
options.rationale: Students who treat each type of radiation as a fixed level of danger drop the size of the dose from the argument.

options.text: The greater dose is certain to cause that person cancer
options.rationale: Chosen by students who state risk as a guaranteed outcome rather than as an increased chance of harm.

mcqs.stem: A worker receives a radiation dose of 2500 mSv. What is this dose in sieverts (Sv)?

options.rationale: The unit is swapped but the number is left unchanged, treating the prefix as a label rather than a factor of 1000.
The student divides by 1000 twice, or confuses milli- with micro-, giving an answer a thousand times too small.
Multiplies by 1000 instead of dividing, because the sievert is remembered as the larger unit.

options.text: 2.5 Sv
options.rationale: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000 to give 2.5 Sv.

mcqs.stem: A table gives these average doses: chest X-ray 0.02 mSv; CT scan of the abdomen 8 mSv; natural background radiation 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: One chest X-ray gives a larger dose than one CT scan
options.rationale: Misreads the table, helped by the fact that X-rays are the more familiar hazard and 0.02 is read without attention to place value.

options.text: A CT scan is certain to cause that patient to get cancer
options.rationale: Turns an increased risk of harm into a certain consequence, which the data cannot support.

options.text: Background radiation is harmless because it is natural
options.rationale: Students equate 'natural' with 'safe' and so discount the background dose entirely when comparing.

options.text: One CT scan gives about three years' worth of background
options.rationale: 8 mSv divided by 2.7 mSv per year is about 3 years, and all three figures are already in the same unit, so the comparison is valid.

mcqs.stem: Worker A receives a dose of 800 mSv in a year. Worker B receives 1.2 Sv in the same year. Who receives the larger dose?

options.text: Neither, because the two doses are equal once converted
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who converts carelessly, or who assumes a question comparing two units must resolve to a tie.

options.text: A, because 800 is a much bigger number than 1.2 is
options.rationale: The numbers are compared directly and the units are treated as labels rather than as part of each value.

options.text: B, because 1.2 Sv is 1200 mSv, more than A's 800 mSv
options.rationale: Using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, B's dose is 1200 mSv, which is greater than A's 800 mSv, so B has the greater risk of harm.

options.text: A, because a millisievert is larger than a sievert is
options.rationale: The factor of 1000 is applied in the wrong direction, making the milli- unit the larger one.

mcqs.stem: Which hazardous effect on the human body is caused by ultraviolet waves?

options.text: Immediate burning of tissue deep inside the body
options.rationale: Assumes every hazardous radiation penetrates deeply, whereas the effects named for ultraviolet are effects on the skin.

options.text: Heating of the whole body from the inside outwards
options.rationale: Heating is the student's general explanation of how any electromagnetic wave harms tissue, carried over from infrared.

options.text: Mutation of genes caused by ionisation of tissue
options.rationale: Applies the X-ray and gamma-ray effect to ultraviolet, because the student links 'cancer' automatically with 'ionising'.

options.text: Premature ageing of the skin and skin cancer risk
options.rationale: Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.

mcqs.stem: Why are X-rays and gamma rays described as hazardous to human body tissue?

options.text: They heat body tissue very quickly, causing severe burns
options.rationale: Heating is transferred from infrared and microwaves and used as the general mechanism of harm.

options.text: They age the skin, but do not reach the deeper tissue
options.rationale: Gives the ultraviolet effect for X-rays and gamma rays, treating all three hazardous waves as doing the same thing.

options.text: They are ionising and can cause gene mutation and cancer
options.rationale: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.

options.text: They travel at very high speed right through the body
options.rationale: Speed is confused with hazard; all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, so this cannot be the reason.
